message.content:
For a **linear** equation  

\[
bx+c=0 ,
\]

the unknown \(x\) appears only with degree 1, so there’s either one unique solution or none/infinitely many depending on the coefficients:

| Condition | Solution |
|-----------|----------|
| \(b \neq 0\) | \(x=-\,\dfrac{c}{b}\) – exactly one real root. |
| \(b = 0,\; c \ne 0\) | No solution (contradiction). |
| \(b = 0,\; c = 0\) | Every real number satisfies the equation (infinite “solutions”). |

---

### Quick derivation  
Starting from \(bx+c=0\):

1. Subtract \(c\): \(bx = -c\).
2. Divide by \(b\) (allowed iff \(b\neq0\)): \(x = -c / b\).

If you plug this back into the original expression it indeed gives zero:
\(b(-c/b)+c = -c + c = 0.\)

That’s all! If you have specific numeric values for \(b\) and \(c\), simply compute \(-c/b\); but remember the edge‑cases above when \(b=0\).
